The paper presents a transparent and data-driven methodology for monitoring the plasma state in a tokamak device.
The approach combines supervised and unsupervised learning techniques.
The dataset used in this work consists of 520 expert-validated discharges from the ILW campaigns at JET.
The state reconstruction task aims to maximize the similarity between the input plasma state and its reconstruction.
The smooth latent movement task enforces smooth trajectory dynamics for consecutive latent variables of a discharge in the latent space.
The reference warning time T predisr is the point in time at which the plasma state is considered to diverge from its expected trajectory to become disruptive.
The dataset split used for training, testing, and validation is 80% for training, 10% for testing, and 10% for validation.
The evaluation metric used for the state-based approach is mean absolute percentage error (MA%) and false alarm rate (FA%).
The evaluation metric used for the sequence-based approach is mean absolute percentage error (MA%) and false alarm rate (FA%).
The performance of the state-based approach in terms of MA% and FA% is 2.39±1.5 and 55.7±6.3, respectively.
The performance of the sequence-based approach in terms of MA% and FA% is 9.54±2.4 and 23.3±3.4, respectively.
The difference between the state-based and sequence-based approaches in terms of MA% and FA% is that the sequence-based approach has a lower MA% and FA% compared to the state-based approach.
The performance of the hybrid detector in terms of missed alarm rate and false alarm rate is zero missed alarm rate and unchanged false alarm rate.
There is a significant correlation between false alarms and labeled precursor events.
The sequence-based approach achieves smoother latent trajectory evolutions compared to the state-based approach.
The standard errors on the supervised tasks for both model types are rather large, likely due to data scarcity regarding samples within the disruptive phases.
The transformer model backbone used in the sequence-based approach is inspired by the GPT-2 architecture, but with a reduced model dimensionality (d = 192) and three attention heads (h = 3).
The AdamW optimizer is used for training the models.
The sequences are sampled with a length of 512 states, spanning approximately one second.
The analysis domain is established from the flat-top start until the boundary condition T is met, avoiding the non-stationary plasma current ramp phase.
The dataset is imbalanced, with a disruptive vs stable state ratio of η = 0.1725 when using T predisr to mark the start of the unstable phase.
The automated labeling of the discharge, including the definition of discharges phases, plasma regime transitions, and precursor events, is handled through the DEFUSE software.
